readerTitle: She owns 70% of the factory. Why can't she buy the machine?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (금속 부품 공장, 앱 스타트업) + 실제 기업 (Meta의 차등의결권, 1985년 Apple 이사회)
insight: 지분율은 '누가 돈을 받는가'를 정할 뿐, '누가 결정하는가'는 의결권·이사회·거부권·역할·영향력이 따로 정한다.
misconception: 51% 이상만 가지면 회사를 마음대로 운영할 수 있다.

sources.text: Meta Platforms, annual proxy statement (Class A / Class B share voting structure)
Apple의 1985년 경영진 교체 (Steve Jobs 운영 역할 박탈 후 퇴사). Walter Isaacson, Steve Jobs (2011) 등 다수 문헌에 기록
공장·앱 스타트업 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Meta: 저커버그가 소수 지분으로 과반 의결권을 가지며 Class B 주식은 주당 10표. 게시 직전 최신 위임장 설명서로 확인하세요. 카드에는 정확한 비율을 쓰지 않았습니다.
Apple 1985: 존 스컬리와의 갈등 뒤 이사회가 잡스의 운영 역할을 박탈했고, 잡스는 같은 해 회사를 떠났습니다. 잡스가 스컬리를 영입했다는 점과, 당시 잡스가 회장이자 대주주였다는 점을 확인하세요.
차트 계산: 이사 5명 중 창업자 2명 = 40%, 투자자 2명 = 40%, 독립이사 1명 = 20%. 지분 55% + 45% = 100%.
의결권, 이사회, 소수주주 보호 규정은 나라와 회사 형태마다 다릅니다. 특정 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 Watch out 카드에 변호사 검토를 권하는 문장을 넣었습니다.

cards.title: She owns 70% of the factory. Why can't she buy the machine?
body: Dana runs a small metal parts shop. She owns 70%. Her partner Lee owns 30%.
Dana wants a new laser cutter, paid for with a bank loan. Lee says no. And Lee wins.

image.label: Factory owner looking at a laser cutter she can't buy
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 금속 가공 공장에서 한 여성이 새 레이저 절단기 앞에 서 있고, 기계에 작은 자물쇠가 걸려 있음. 벽의 파이 차트에는 70%와 30%가 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're bringing in a partner.
body: You run a parts shop alone. A partner offers cash and shop-floor experience in exchange for a share of the business.
You want to stay in charge. What do you focus on in the deal?

options.text: Keep at least 51%, so you always have the majority
options.feedback: A majority helps in a vote. But other clauses in the agreement can still let a 30% owner block your biggest decisions.

options.text: Agree in writing which decisions need whose approval
options.feedback: It means hard conversations now. But it settles who actually runs the shop, which percentages alone don't.

options.text: Keep 80% and give the partner a smaller stake
options.feedback: You keep more of the profits. Your partner can still gain power through vetoes or the customers they bring in.

cards.title: What Dana signed.
body: When Lee joined, Dana kept 70%. She also agreed to one clause: any loan over $100,000 needs both partners' approval. It seemed fair, since Lee was putting in money.
Lee also runs the shop floor and handles the biggest customer. If Lee walked out, that customer might follow.
So Dana owns **most of the value**. Lee holds much of the say on big moves.

cards.title: Ownership vs control
body: **Ownership** is your claim on the value: a share of the profits, and of the money if the business is sold. **Control** is who gets to decide.
By default they travel together: one share, one vote. But they can be pulled apart, on purpose or by accident, and often in a single clause.

image.label: A coin and a steering wheel held by different hands
image.brief: 두 손을 나란히 그린 일러스트. 왼손은 큰 동전 더미("Ownership: who gets the money"), 오른손은 운전대("Control: who decides")를 잡고 있음. 두 손이 서로 다른 사람의 것임을 소매 색으로 구분.

cards.title: Where control actually comes from.
body: Control comes from several places besides your percentage:
list: **Votes:** some shares carry extra votes, some carry none
**Board seats:** the board can hire and fire the person in charge
**Vetoes:** clauses that require a minority owner's yes
**The job:** who runs things day to day
**Leverage:** who holds key customers, skills or know-how
cards.callout: Check all five, not just the percentage.

cards.title: An app company where the majority isn't in charge.
body: After two funding rounds, two founders own 55% of their app company. Investors own 45%.
The five-person board has two founders, two investors and one independent member. The founders own the majority, but on the board the **independent director** casts the deciding vote.

image.label: An app company where the majority isn't in charge.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: It cuts both ways.
body: At Meta, Mark Zuckerberg owns a minority of the shares but controls a majority of the votes. His class of shares carries ten votes each. That gives him **control beyond his ownership**.

At Apple in 1985, co-founder Steve Jobs was a major shareholder. After a clash with the CEO he had recruited, the board removed him from his operating role, and he left. His stake didn't protect his job.

image.label: A small share pie next to a large vote pie
image.brief: 두 장면을 좌우로 배치. 왼쪽: 작은 지분 조각을 든 사람이 커다란 '투표' 파이를 쥐고 있음. 오른쪽: 큰 지분 조각을 든 사람이 회의실 문 밖으로 나가는 모습. 실제 기업 로고나 인물 얼굴은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Splitting the two has costs.
body: When someone decides but carries little of the gain or loss, their choices can drift from what the owners want.
Vetoes exist for good reasons. They protect minority owners from being treated unfairly, and investors usually need some. Too many, and the business stalls in deadlock.
Rules on votes, boards and minority rights differ by country and company type. Have a lawyer read any agreement before you sign.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: Your app company is raising money. An investor offers $2 million for 25%.
They also want a board seat, plus a veto over future fundraising, selling the company, yearly budgets and senior hires. What do you do?

options.text: Sign it. You still own 75%, so you're in charge
options.feedback: You keep most of the value but hand over many big decisions. Vetoes on budgets and hiring reach into how you run the business every day.

options.text: Accept the price, but limit vetoes to selling the company and issuing new shares
options.feedback: The investor stays protected against the moves that could hurt them most, and you keep running the business. It may take a tougher negotiation.

options.text: Refuse every veto and the board seat
options.feedback: You keep full control. But many investors won't put in money without some protection, so you may lose the deal.

cards.title: Owning a business and running it are two different things.
body: Before you sign any deal, ask two questions: who gets the money, and who gets to decide?
**Try it today:** list the five biggest decisions in your business. Next to each, write who can approve it and who can block it.
